unit.title: Establish and maintain a strategic planning cycle

summary: This unit teaches you to establish and maintain a strategic planning cycle in a public body: to understand the stages and the planning calendar; to analyse the environment with tools such as PESTLE and SWOT and to consult stakeholders; to set vision, mission, objectives and priorities; to build a results framework with baselines, indicators and targets; to link plans to budgets and cascade them to staff; and to monitor, review and evaluate the plan so that it stays alive.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. **Strategic planning** is how an organisation decides where it is going over the next few years, and how it will get there. A **strategic planning cycle** makes this a regular, repeated process: analyse, set direction, plan and budget, carry out, monitor, evaluate, and then use what was learned in the next round. At Level 5 you set up and run the cycle for a ministry, agency, municipal corporation, school, hotel or business.

Public bodies in Jamaica plan within the Government's financial year and budget process, and their plans should support the country's long-term national development plan, **Vision 2030 Jamaica**. A plan that is not linked to the budget, to results and to people's work soon ends up on the shelf. The aim of this unit is to prevent that.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Explain the cycle and its calendar
Describe the stages, the levels of plan, the roles and how the calendar fits the financial year and the budget process.
Use PESTLE, SWOT, scenarios and stakeholder analysis, and review the body's own capacity.
Write vision, mission, values and objectives, and choose priorities using agreed criteria.
Use a results chain, baselines, indicators, targets and a results framework.
Prepare operational plans and budgets, cascade the plan, manage risk and communicate it.
Report each quarter, run a mid-year review, deal with delays and shocks, and keep the plan current.
Judge what was achieved and why, report to the public, and record lessons for the next cycle.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions, including short sums on percentages, targets and budget shares.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as SWOT, baseline, variance, results framework) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks**: build a planning calendar, a results framework and a monitoring report for a made-up public body.

blocks.note: Learn the order of the stages, the difference between output and outcome, and how to work out the percentage of a planned improvement. These are tested often.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The planning cycle and its calendar

blocks.p: Planning is described as a **cycle** because results feed back into the next round of planning. It is not a one-off event or a document copied out again each year. The purpose is to link direction, plans, budgets and results, and to review them regularly.

flow: Analyse the environment and the body's own position
Set direction: vision, mission, values, objectives
Plan: strategies, priorities, operational plans, budget
Evaluate and review, then start the next round

blocks.p: Signing off petty cash vouchers is routine finance work, not a stage of the planning cycle.

head: Level
Period
What it does
Who prepares it
rows: National plan (Vision 2030 Jamaica and medium-term frameworks)
Sets national goals and priorities that ministries support
Sets the body's direction, objectives, priorities and targets
Executive team or board, with the planning unit
Sets the year's activities, targets, owners and budget
Divisions, compiled by the planning unit
Set each team's and each officer's tasks and targets

ul: A strategic plan **sets direction**; an operational plan **sets the year's work**.
A plan with **no link to national priorities** may not support what the country has agreed to achieve.
A plan that looks only one month or one week ahead is not strategic; one that looks 25 years ahead is too far to manage.

blocks.h: The financial year and the planning calendar

blocks.p: The Government of Jamaica's financial year runs from **1 April to 31 March**. Ministries prepare their budget submissions during the months before it starts, and the Estimates of Expenditure are then laid before Parliament. The **planning calendar** is the schedule that sets the dates for each step of the planning and reporting cycle.

ul: Set the calendar to match the budget cycle, so that priorities and operational plans are ready **in time to shape the budget bids**. A plan written after the budget is spent has no effect.
Include dates for environmental analysis, consultation, drafting, approval, budget submission, quarterly reports, the mid-year review, the annual report and the evaluation.

head: Example calendar (financial year starting 1 April)
Typical timing
rows: Environmental analysis and review of last year
Plan approved and shared with staff

blocks.note: These dates are an example. Use the actual dates in your own body's calendar and the finance ministry's budget circulars.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Who
Role
rows: Approves the strategic direction and the plan (in a statutory body, the board normally approves the plan after the executive team has prepared it)
Sets direction, agrees priorities and owns the plan. It must not leave the work to the planning unit or sign without reading
Coordinates the process, sets and runs the calendar, supplies templates and compiles reports. It does not write every division's plan or make policy choices
Prepare operational plans, deliver them and report
Carry out work plans and give front-line knowledge
Costs the plans and links them to the budget

blocks.p: Write down the planning procedure, calendar and templates. This lets the cycle **run the same way even when staff change**, and stops divisions skipping steps they find inconvenient. Gain the support of the chief executive and board first.
An **environmental scan** is a study of changes outside the organisation that may affect its work. **PESTLE** gives a checklist.

head: Letter
Factor
Examples for a parish municipal corporation
rows: National policies, local government changes, priorities of the Minister
Local job market, inflation, income from fees and property taxes, donor funding
Population growth, ageing, crime, new housing schemes, public expectations
Online payment, mobile apps, new equipment
New laws on waste, data protection, procurement, employment
Flooding, hurricanes, drought, waste and pollution

head: Position
Helpful
Harmful
rows: **Strengths**: skilled staff, strong partnerships, good reputation
**Weaknesses**: outdated case system that slows service, low skills in data analysis, poor facilities
**Opportunities**: new government funding policy, rising demand for online services, a partner offering shared facilities
**Threats**: budget cuts, hurricanes, new competitors, new laws that add costs

blocks.p: Strengths and weaknesses are **inside** the body and can be changed by it. Opportunities and threats are **outside** and must be anticipated. Use the SWOT to make choices: build on strengths, fix weaknesses that block priorities, use opportunities and protect against threats.

**Scenario planning** tests how a strategy would hold up under different possible futures, such as strong or weak economic growth, or a severe hurricane season. It does not predict the exact future, and it does not remove the need for review or targets.

blocks.h: Looking at the body's own capacity

blocks.p: Before finalising the plan, ask: **do we have the money, staff and skills to deliver it?** Capacity includes people, skills, systems, equipment, buildings and funding. A plan that asks more than the body can deliver will fail.

Consult staff, partner agencies, service users and other stakeholders. Their views improve the plan and build support for it. It does not mean the senior team need not decide anything, and it does not mean every citizen approves the plan.

head: Power / interest
Stakeholder type
How to manage
rows: A donor or the finance ministry
Keep satisfied with regular, targeted updates

blocks.note: Ignoring a high-power stakeholder, or sending them unexplained data files, will cost you support later. Send short, relevant updates.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Element
What it is
Example
rows: Forward-looking picture of what the body wants to become or achieve in the long term
A healthy, safe and prosperous parish for all
A short statement of what the body does and for whom, now
We provide safe, reliable water to homes and businesses
How staff behave in carrying out the plan
A broad result to be achieved within the plan period
Improve access to clean water in rural communities
A measurable level of performance by a set date
90% of rural households with piped water by March 2029

blocks.p: Values do not replace measurable targets and do not tell staff which projects to fund first. They guide how people behave.

There are always more good ideas than money. Choose priorities using **agreed criteria**, not the seniority of the person proposing the project, last year's list or cost alone. Typical criteria: fit with national and body goals, impact on the public, legal duty, cost, risk, readiness and capacity.
Give each criterion a weight, score each project, multiply and add.
Y scores slightly higher, although X has the greater impact. A narrow result should be discussed by the executive; the scores support judgement, they do not replace it.

blocks.note: A plan with 28 "top priority" goals has no priorities. Too many spread effort and money too thinly. Keep to a small number of clear objectives.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Record the main risks to achieving the objectives in a **strategic risk register** linked to the plan, with the likelihood, effect, response and owner of each. Not in personal diaries or informal minutes. Review it each quarter.

flow: Impact: the long-term change in society

head: Level
Example: a youth skills programme
rows: A budget of J$150,000,000, trainers, training centres
Recruit young people, run courses, arrange work placements
1,500 young people complete a certified course; 20 courses held; 1,000 manuals printed
More young people in the two parishes find jobs; employers report better skills
Lower youth unemployment in the country over time

blocks.p: Outputs are what the programme produces (people trained, sessions held, manuals printed). **Outcomes** are the changes that follow (crop yields rose, more people found work). Do not report outputs as if they were outcomes.

ul: A **baseline** is the starting level, measured before the target is set. Before you set a target to cut the time to issue permits, find out the current average time.

An **indicator** is a measure that shows progress, such as the share of customers served within 20 minutes. A good indicator is clearly defined, measurable, relevant and has a data source. The number of computers bought or meetings held does not show whether service has improved.
A **target** is a measurable level to be reached by a set date.
A **results framework** is the table that lists each objective with its indicators, baselines, targets, data sources and owners.

head: Objective
Indicator
Baseline
Target
Source
Owner
rows: % of Grade 4 pupils reading at the national standard

blocks.p: To judge progress, compare the change achieved with the change planned: **(latest - baseline) / (target - baseline) x 100**.

head: Example
Working
rows: Birth registrations within 30 days: baseline 60%, target 80%, latest 72%
Processing time cut from 30 to 21 days

blocks.p: Note that the first two are percentages of the **improvement planned**, not the percentage level reached. A body halfway through a plan period and 50% of the way to its target is on track.

If halfway through the year an agency has completed 45% of its annual inspections target, it is a little behind (about 50% would be expected if work is spread evenly). Management should check whether it can catch up, and not conclude that it has failed or relax.

An operational plan takes the strategy for one financial year. For each objective it lists activities, targets, owners, dates, resources and the budget. It is prepared by divisions and compiled by the planning unit.
A plan without a budget is a wish list, and a budget without a plan spends money without purpose. Link them:

ul: Agree priorities and operational plans **before** budget submissions are prepared.
Cost every activity. Targets must be realistic for the money available.
If a division asks for money for a project that is not in the plan, ask how it fits the plan or put it through a review. Do not fund it quietly or cut other projects without a review.
Show the budget by strategic objective, so that the executive can see what each goal will cost.

blocks.h: Sharing a budget by ratio and percentage

head: Example
Working
rows: J$2,700,000,000 shared among three goals in the ratio 5 : 3 : 1
12% of a J$750,000,000 capital budget for a digital goal
6 parts; one part = J$400,000,000; first goal J$1,200,000,000

blocks.note: Check ratio sums by adding the shares: 1,500 + 900 + 300 = 2,700 million. Work every sum twice.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Individual work plans and appraisal targets

ul: Objectives reach officers **through division plans, unit plans and work plans**, not through one email, only through speeches or only to senior managers.
Link officers' appraisal targets to the plan, so that what is rewarded is what the plan needs.
After approval, communicate the plan: briefings, a short summary, and links to unit plans. Do not just store it on a shared drive.

blocks.p: Check money, staff, skills, systems and facilities. If capacity is missing, include building it in the plan (for example training, recruitment or a new system).

sections.title: Monitoring, reviewing and keeping the plan alive

ul: Management reviews progress on the operational plan **each quarter**, with a fuller **mid-year review**.

Each division submits a short report on one template: progress on each indicator and activity, spending against budget, **variance** (the gap between planned and actual), reasons and corrective action.
The planning unit checks the data, asks for evidence and compiles a summary.
Agree **definitions and data sources** for each indicator, so that results from different divisions can be added up and compared.

head: Status
Meaning
Typical response
rows: Results are at or close to the target
Agree corrective action and a date to recheck
Escalate to the executive; review the target, resources or approach

blocks.p: A three-colour dashboard like this shows at a glance which objectives are on track, at risk or off track.

An annual target of 1,200 inspections, with 540 done by the end of September (six months into the financial year): 540 / 1,200 x 100 = 45%. An operational plan with 40 activities of which 34 are complete is 85% complete. Always compare the percentage with the share of the year that has passed.

ul: A key project is three months behind: the planning unit **flags it, finds the cause and agrees action with the project owner**. It does not leave it out of the report, change the target to look on track or wait for the annual review.
The risk register is updated each quarter.

blocks.p: A **rolling plan** is updated each year, with a new year added at the end, so that it always looks several years ahead. Update the plan in between when something major happens, such as a national emergency that reduces the budget, a major hurricane or a change in government priorities. Review priorities against agreed criteria; do not cut every programme by the same percentage, do not carry on as if nothing has changed and do not wait for the end of the plan period.
The **annual report** reports results against the plan to the public, Parliament and other stakeholders. It does not replace the operational plan and is not written before the plan.

At the end of the plan period, evaluate what was achieved and why, so as to inform the next plan. The aim is to learn, not to find someone to blame and not to prove that everything was met. Record the lessons and review them as the next cycle begins; do not start from a blank page.

blocks.h: Why plans end up on the shelf

blocks.p: Too many vague priorities; targets with no baselines or owners; no link to the budget; weak communication; no regular review. To keep the plan alive: few clear priorities with named owners, a link to budget and appraisals, regular meetings that discuss the plan, honest reporting, and quick updates when circumstances change.

tell outputs from outcomes.

review and update the plan when circumstances change.

terms: Strategic planning cycle
The repeated process of analysing, setting direction, planning, implementing, monitoring and evaluating.
Vision 2030 Jamaica
Jamaica's long-term national development plan, which ministries' plans should support.
Planning calendar
The schedule that sets the dates for each step of the planning and reporting cycle.
Environmental scan
A study of outside changes that may affect the organisation's work.
SWOT
Strengths and weaknesses (inside) set beside opportunities and threats (outside).
PESTLE
Political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors.
Vision
The forward-looking statement of what an organisation wants to become or achieve.
Mission
A short statement of what an organisation does and for whom.
Operational plan
The yearly plan of a division's activities, targets and budget.
Results chain
Inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact.
Baseline
The starting level before a target is set.
Target
A measurable level of performance to be reached by a set date.
Results framework
The table listing each objective with its indicators, baselines, targets and data sources.
Variance
The gap between planned and actual results or spending.
Rolling plan
A plan updated each year with a new year added at the end.
Capacity
An organisation's ability, in staff, skills, systems and money, to deliver its plan.

c1.title: A new youth skills agency
c1.text: A new national agency for youth skills has been set up with a board and a chief executive, Mrs Heather Campbell. The board wants to start by writing objectives at once, because the Minister is waiting for a plan. Budget submissions for the next financial year are due on 15 November. Draft objectives so far have no named owners.

c2.title: A municipal corporation scans its environment
c2.text: A municipal corporation in Portland begins its planning cycle. A new national law will require all local authorities to separate waste. Residents are asking for online payment of fees, which the corporation cannot yet offer. Residents' associations are keenly interested in the plan but have little formal power. The Mayor and the chief executive have both.

c3.title: A literacy programme
c3.text: A ministry's plan for the four years from April 2026 has a results framework for primary reading. The indicator is the percentage of Grade 4 pupils reading at the national standard. The baseline is 52%, the target is 70% by March 2030, and the latest result, at the end of year two, is 61%. The programme has trained 120 teachers and delivered 8,000 reading books.

c4.title: Budget and priorities in a ministry
c4.text: A ministry has J$2,700,000,000 to share among three strategic goals in the ratio 5 : 3 : 1. Within its capital budget of J$750,000,000, 12% is set aside for the digital goal. Two proposed projects are scored on impact (50%), fit with plan (30%) and cost (20%). Project X scores 9, 6 and 3; Project Y scores 6, 8 and 8. The draft plan lists activities, but none of them has a cost.

c5.title: A mid-year review at an agency
c5.text: An agency's operational plan for the year starting 1 April has 80 activities. At the end of September, 28 are complete. The new Minister has announced a new priority, youth employment, in the middle of the plan period. The chief executive says the plan was approved last year and it is time to move on to the next one.

questions.q: The board wants to write objectives immediately. What has been left out?
o: A decision on the colour and design of the plan's cover and its printing
A list of every officer who will work on the plan in future years
An analysis of the environment and the agency's baseline position
The date of the annual report to the public after the first year
questions.why: Objectives should come from an analysis of the environment, capacity and current performance. Without it the targets may be unrealistic or irrelevant.

questions.q: Budget submissions are due on 15 November. When should the agency agree its priorities and operational plans?
o: Before the submissions are prepared, so the plans shape the bids
After the budget is approved, so that the figures are known
In January, once the new financial year has started
At the mid-year review, when progress is known
questions.why: The planning calendar must match the budget cycle. Plans agreed after the budget is spent cannot influence what money is requested.

questions.q: Why should each draft objective have a named owner?
o: So that the owner can be blamed for any target that is missed
So that other divisions need not take part in the work
So that the planning unit can avoid monitoring the objective
So that one senior person is accountable for delivery and reporting
questions.why: An owner gives clear accountability, so progress is reported and problems are raised. It does not remove the need for others to contribute.

questions.q: Which statement belongs in the agency's vision?
o: Train 3,000 young people by March 2028
A skilled and employed young population across Jamaica
Run twenty courses in each parish each year
Spend J$50,000,000 on training equipment next year
questions.why: A vision is a long-term picture of what the body wants to achieve. The others are a target, an activity and a budget item.

questions.q: The new waste separation law is an example of which PESTLE factor?
o: Political
Economic
Legal
Technological
questions.why: A change in law is a legal factor. A national policy decision could also be political, but a requirement set by law is classed as legal.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis, how should the residents' demand for online payment be classified?
o: An opportunity, because it is outside the corporation and could help it
A strength, because it shows that residents are interested in services
A weakness, because the corporation cannot yet offer it
A threat, because it will increase the work of the staff
questions.why: Demand from residents is an external factor that the corporation can use, so it is an opportunity. Not yet offering online payment is a weakness, which is internal.

questions.q: The residents' associations have high interest and little power. How should the planning team treat them?
o: Manage them closely and give them the final say on the plan's contents
Monitor them through general public notices and nothing more
Ignore them until the plan has been completed and approved
Keep them informed and consult them as the plan is developed
questions.why: Stakeholders with high interest but low power should be informed and consulted. Their knowledge improves the plan and builds support.

questions.q: The SWOT shows a weakness: the corporation has no reliable data on road conditions. How should the plan use this?
o: Leave it out of the plan, since a plan should show only strengths
Make building the data an objective or action, if it blocks other goals
List it as a threat that comes from outside the corporation
Wait for the next planning cycle before starting to look at it
questions.why: A SWOT is used to make choices. A weakness that blocks priorities should be tackled in the plan, and it is an internal factor, not a threat.

questions.q: What percentage of the planned improvement has been achieved at the end of year two?
questions.why: (61 - 52) / (70 - 52) = 9 / 18 = 50%. The level reached, 61%, is not the percentage of the planned improvement.

questions.q: Is the programme on track? The plan period is four years.
o: Yes, 50% of the planned improvement after half of the period
No, because the target of 70% has not yet been reached
No, because only 61% of pupils are reading at standard
Yes, because 120 teachers have been trained so far
questions.why: After two of four years, half of the planned improvement is on track, if the pace holds. Teachers trained is an output and does not itself show progress.

questions.q: Which result is an outcome rather than an output?
o: 120 teachers complete training
8,000 reading books are delivered
Twelve workshops are held in four parishes
The share of pupils reading at standard rises
questions.why: An outcome is a change that follows the work. Teachers trained, books delivered and workshops held are outputs.

questions.q: Which is the best indicator for the objective of improving reading?
o: The number of reading books on the shelves of school libraries
The percentage of Grade 4 pupils reading at the national standard
The number of ministry staff who work in the literacy unit
The number of literacy meetings that the ministry has held
questions.why: A good indicator measures the result sought, can be checked against a data source and is not simply a count of effort.

questions.q: How much of the J$2,700,000,000 goes to the first goal, in the ratio 5 : 3 : 1?
questions.why: 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 parts, so one part is J$300,000,000, and five parts are J$1,500,000,000. Check: 1,500 + 900 + 300 = 2,700 million.

questions.q: What share of the J$2,700,000,000 goes to the second goal, in the ratio 5 : 3 : 1?
o: About 33%
About 60%
About 11%
About 50%
questions.why: The second goal has 3 of the 9 parts: 3 / 9 = 33.3%, or J$900,000,000. Check: 33.3% of J$2,700,000,000 is J$900,000,000.

questions.q: After weighting, Project X scores 6.9 and Project Y scores 7.0. How should the executive use these scores?
o: As the final decision, since the highest score always wins the vote
As proof that the two projects are equal, so one may be chosen by lot
As a reason to fund neither project until the next planning cycle
As a guide: discuss the narrow gap and record the reasons for the choice
questions.why: Scores support judgement; they do not replace it. A narrow gap should be discussed, and the reasons for the decision recorded, so that it is open and fair.

questions.q: None of the activities in the draft plan has a cost. What is the main problem?
o: The plan will be too short for the board to approve it at all
Targets may be unrealistic and cannot be linked to the budget
The plan will not need any monitoring during the whole year
The plan cannot be sent to Parliament with the budget papers
questions.why: Costing each activity allows the plan to be linked to the budget and shows whether the targets are realistic for the resources available.

questions.q: At the end of September, 28 of the 80 activities are complete. What percentage is that, and what does it show?
o: 35%, so the agency is well ahead of its schedule for the year
28%, so the agency has completed more than a quarter of its work
35%, so the agency is behind the pace expected after six months
44%, so the agency is about on track for the full year
questions.why: 28 / 80 x 100 = 35%. Six months, about half of the year, have passed, so around 50% would be expected if work is spread evenly.

questions.q: Which tool best shows at a glance which objectives are on track, at risk or off track?
o: A dashboard with green, amber and red status
The full text of the operational plan
The list of staff who attended planning meetings
The ministry's annual report from the previous year
questions.why: A status dashboard turns the data into a quick signal for managers. The other documents do not show current progress.

questions.q: The new Minister announces a youth employment priority in mid-plan. What should the agency do?
o: Carry on as if nothing had changed until the plan period ends
Add the new priority to the plan and leave everything else the same
Cancel the existing plan and start a completely new one from nothing
Review priorities against its criteria and update the plan and budget
questions.why: A major change calls for a review of priorities and an update of the plan and budget, so the new priority is funded and affordable.

questions.q: The chief executive says the plan was approved and it is time to move on. Which routine best keeps the plan alive?
o: An annual reminder email asking all divisions to read the whole plan
Quarterly reviews where heads report against the plan and the executive acts
A printed copy of the plan placed on every manager's desk
A single review of the plan at the end of the plan period
questions.why: Regular reviews with reports against the plan, decisions and follow-up keep the plan in use. Passive circulation or a single end review lets it go on the shelf.
